sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: The accusative marks the person or thing that receives the action.

blocks.text: In "Ich sehe den Hund", the dog is the direct object: it is what I see. German marks that role with the accusative case. Only masculine articles change: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen.

Feminine, neuter and plural articles keep their nominative form in the accusative: die Frau, das Kind, die Kinder. Pronouns change too: mich, dich, ihn and sie replace ich, du, er and sie when they are the object.

blocks.title: One change to remember
blocks.text: If the noun is masculine and it is the direct object, use den or einen. Everything else stays as you already know it.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

rows: Ich öffne die Tür und das Fenster.

items: Ask "Wen oder was?" (whom or what?) to find the direct object.
The accusative does not change feminine, neuter or plural articles.
Use ihn for a masculine person or thing, and sie for a feminine one.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

items.hint: The final d in Hund sounds like a t: hunt.
Start with the "eye" sound: EI-nen, not EE-nen.
The ch after i is soft, like the h in "hue".

blocks.text: Dogs are common in German towns and on public transport, but rules vary. Many shops and restaurants allow dogs, while others ask you to wait outside.
On trains, a small dog often travels free, while a larger dog may need its own ticket. Asking "Ist der Hund hier erlaubt?" is always a safe start.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: Read the scene, then play it and follow the speakers.
sections.setting: At a pet shop, Anna wants a new ball for her dog.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.de: Guten Tag, ich brauche einen Ball für meinen Hund.
lines.en: Hello, I need a ball for my dog.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.de: Der Hund ist klein. Haben Sie einen kleinen Ball?
lines.en: The dog is small. Do you have a small ball?

lines.speaker: Verkäufer
lines.de: Ja, diesen hier. Er kostet vier Euro.
lines.en: Yes, this one here. It costs four euros.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Accusative articles at a glance
sections.lede: The direct object is the person or thing affected by the verb.

blocks.text: The question "Wen oder was?" tests for the accusative. If the answer is masculine, the article changes.

sections.tip: Learn the pair der/den and ein/einen together. The other articles stay the same.

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Choose the answer that fits the sentence or the rule.

exercises.explanation: Hund is masculine and the direct object, so der becomes den.
Tisch is masculine and the direct object, so ein becomes einen.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun replaces "den Mann" in "Ich sehe den Mann"?
exercises.explanation: The masculine direct object pronoun is ihn.
The direct object form of du is dich.

sections.title: Complete the sentence

exercises.explanation: Bruder is masculine and the direct object of haben, so use einen.
Film is masculine and the direct object, so der becomes den.

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Click the words in the order that makes a correct German sentence.

exercises.explanation: The verb comes second, and the masculine direct object takes den.
Kauft is the verb in second position; einen marks the masculine object.
A yes/no question starts with the verb, followed by the subject and object.

questions.prompt: What is the customer looking for?
questions.explanation: The customer says "Ich suche einen Mantel", and Mantel means coat.

questions.prompt: How much does the coat cost?
questions.explanation: The seller says "sechzig Euro", which is sixty euros.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Say what you see in your room and what you need today. Use den or einen at least once.

model.de: Ich sehe den Tisch. Ich brauche einen neuen Stuhl.
model.en: I see the table. I need a new chair.

tips: Say the sentence once slowly, then once at normal speed.
Check that every masculine object has den or einen.
Use "Ich brauche …" to add a second sentence without extra grammar.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.why: The direct object is masculine, so der must become den.
Bruder is masculine and the object of haben, so ein becomes einen.
Use the accusative pronoun ihn, not the subject pronoun er.
